title: GIAC GCFA
summary: The GIAC Certified Forensic Analyst (GCFA) is an advanced, hands on certification for analysts who investigate compromised computers and prove what happened on them. It suits incident responders, threat hunters, forensic examiners and experienced SOC analysts who already read host data as part of their job. It proves to an employer that you can collect volatile evidence, analyse memory, rebuild a file system timeline, spot anti forensic tricks, and write findings that would survive scrutiny in a formal investigation. The exam is a proctored, open book test built around performance based and multiple choice items, so you work with real artefacts rather than recalling definitions. GIAC does not publish domain weightings, so none appear below. It leads to digital forensics, incident response and threat hunting roles. This is an independent study guide and it is not affiliated with GIAC or SANS.

beginner.definition: The GCFA is a certification from GIAC about digital forensics. Digital forensics means investigating computers after a security incident to find out what happened. This certification focuses on host evidence, such as memory and file system records. It looks at that evidence rather than at network traffic. It is an advanced certification for people who already work in security. The exam is open book, so your own notes are allowed.
beginner.whyItMatters: When a serious breach happens, someone must produce facts that stand up to challenge. Guesses are not enough. This certification proves you can work that way with real evidence. It is one of the most respected credentials in incident response. It therefore opens senior roles and specialist teams. The open book format rewards careful preparation, so the notes you build stay useful after the exam.
howItWorks: Build a practice lab with test machines that you own. You must examine systems without damaging the evidence.
Learn the order of volatility. Collect the most fragile evidence, such as memory, before anything else.
Study each artefact type in turn. Learn what it can prove and what it cannot prove.
Practise building a timeline from several artefact sources. Explain how the events fit together.
Index your notes with tabs and a contents page, because you may use them during the exam.
The exam itself is proctored and open book. It uses performance based items alongside multiple choice questions.
beginner.example: Imagine a manager's laptop that ran slowly for two weeks. It then sent data to an unknown address. You cannot simply reinstall the system. The evidence lives in memory, in prefetch records that show which programs ran, and in file timestamps. You copy memory first, then the disk. Later you line up every timestamp in order. You see a program that ran once, deleted itself, and opened a network connection. That reconstructed story is the deliverable, not the tool you used.
takeaways: Collect the most fragile evidence first, because memory disappears when power goes off.
Every artefact proves some things and stays silent about others, so never overclaim.
Take detailed notes and index them, because the exam is open book.

objectives: Explain the difference between volatile and non volatile evidence and why the order of collection matters.
Collect memory and disk evidence in a way that keeps it trustworthy and repeatable.
Analyse memory to identify running processes, network connections and injected code.
Interpret Windows artefacts such as registry keys, prefetch records and event logs.
Build a timeline from several artefact sources and explain the sequence of activity it shows.
Recognise anti forensic techniques and describe how to detect them anyway.

chapters.title: Enterprise Environment Incident Response
objectives: Describe how an incident response process works in a large organisation with many systems.
Explain how to scope a compromise by checking other hosts for the same evidence.
Describe how threat hunting finds activity that no alert has reported yet.
Explain how findings from a forensic case feed back into detection and hardening.

chapters.title: Introduction to Memory Forensics
objectives: Capture memory from a running system correctly and record how the capture was made.
Use memory analysis tools to list processes, loaded modules and network connections.
Identify suspicious or hidden processes in a memory image and explain your reasoning.
Explain what memory analysis can prove that disk analysis alone cannot.

chapters.title: Analyzing Volatile Malicious Event Artifacts
objectives: Look for evidence of code running only in memory without a file on disk.
Identify injected code and explain how it hides inside a legitimate process.
Identify suspicious network connections in memory and judge whether they are malicious.
Explain how a rootkit alters what the operating system reports about itself.

chapters.title: Analyzing Volatile Windows Event Artifacts
objectives: Interpret Windows event logs and identify the entries that matter during an investigation.
Describe what a system's volatile state shows about recent user and process activity.
Correlate several volatile artefacts to support a single conclusion.
Explain how to preserve volatile evidence before a reboot destroys it.

chapters.title: Introduction to File System Timeline Forensics
objectives: Describe how file system timestamps are created, changed and updated.
Explain why timestamps alone can mislead an analyst who ignores how they are set.
Build a timeline from file system metadata and describe the period it covers.
Present a timeline in a way that another analyst can follow and check.

chapters.title: File System Timeline Artifact Analysis
objectives: Combine timestamps from several sources into one ordered timeline.
Identify gaps and contradictions in a timeline and explain what each one suggests.
Identify the point in the timeline when an attacker first gained access.
Explain how to state the limits of a timeline without overstating what it proves.

chapters.title: NTFS Artifact Analysis
objectives: Explain how the NTFS file system records files, directories and their metadata.
Use file system records to recover information about deleted files.
Interpret alternate data streams and explain why malware uses them.
Explain how to prove that a file existed even when it has been removed.

chapters.title: Windows Artifact Analysis
objectives: Interpret registry keys that show what programs and devices were used on a system.
Interpret program execution artefacts and explain what each one proves.
Interpret artefacts that show file and folder access by a user.
Reconstruct how a user or an attacker interacted with a host from several artefact types.

chapters.title: Identification of Normal System and User Activity
objectives: Describe what ordinary activity looks like on a Windows host so that anomalies stand out.
Explain how software updates and administration tasks leave traces that can look suspicious.
Distinguish expected behaviour from malicious behaviour using supporting evidence.
Explain why you must establish a baseline before you can call activity unusual.

chapters.title: Identification of Malicious System and User Activity
objectives: Identify persistence mechanisms that keep malware running after a reboot.
Recognise anti forensic techniques such as timestamp alteration and log clearing.
Explain how an attacker moves between systems and what trace that movement leaves.
Describe how to confirm that a malicious foothold has been fully removed.
